catalog_quote: Stress has been posited for Isthmus Zapotec; it affects the length of the vowel itself (before lenis consonants), or the length of the consonant that follows (if it is fortis), or the tone (see Conventions). It usually falls on the penultimate (or the only) syllable of the root when the vowels are modal, although there are exceptions. Convincing examples clearly showing that the generalization is not appropriately stated as referring to the first syllable of the root are not easy to come by since stems longer than two syllables often seem to be compounds or to derive from compounds. The word /wakaaba/ ... ‘a particularly venomous tarantula’ may be an appropriate example. The weight of a syllable also affects the placement of stress. Final diphthongs attract stress: ... ‘reed (otate)’. Final laryngealized vowels also attract stress: ... ‘woman’. Stress does not occur on the prefix of a w…
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title, Pickett 1951 (word 7: 60-65), the article previously marked 'cited in the JIPA references; not opened' and 'could not be reached by automated download'. The publisher copy is still could not be reached by automated download, but the Internet Archive Serials-in-Microfilm scan of word 7(1) (sim_word_1951-04_7_1, unrestricted, text) was downloaded; the whole issue, its scanned text, and an extracted six-page PDF plus text of the article are and logged in and md5sums recorded). Read in full: stress is predictable over the grammatical word, falling on the unique heavy (complex-nucleus) syllable in any position, else on the penult; short vowel + fortis consonant counts as heavy (VV); tone is irrelevant; loans get penult or last-closed-syllable stress. Bears on the catalog: REFINES the 'weight-hedged' coding (deciding source JIPA 2010 by the same Pickett with Marlett): it supplies the explicit weight algorithm behind JIPA's hedge and agrees with all of JIPA's clauses, so the classification stands; the catalog's source note should change from 'not opened' to read, and Pickett 1951 should be cited as the primary support for the weight clause. It does not supersede JIPA 2010 as the deciding source (later, same author, adds root-domain and clitic facts). Still unread for this language and outside this search of works with stress in the title's items: Mock 1988 (doi:10.1515/9783110874266.197, paywalled) and Marlett & Pickett 1987 (doi:10.1086/466066, paywalled). all discovery here was via Crossref, Unpaywall and the archive.org search API.

new_statements.quote: Stress falls (1) on the syllable containing a complex nucleus in words with one and only one such syllable, (2) on the penultimate syllable (a) in words containing two or more syllables each with complex nucleus and (b) in words containing only open syllables each with simple nucleus, (3) on the last closed syllable of words with no syllable of complex nucleus but with one or more closed syllables. Thus we conclude that for both words of native origin and loan words, stress is predictable in Isthmus Zapotec.
new_statements.citation: Pickett, Velma B. 1951. Nonphonemic stress: a problem in stress placement in Isthmus Zapotec. word 7(1): 60-65. doi:10.1080/00437956.1951.11659392
new_statements.locator: p. 65, the italicised 'combination statement' and the following conclusion (p. 6 of the extracted file = scan page 69 of); supporting: p. 61 tentative rule and fn. 5 (nucleus types), pp. 62-64 (short V + fortis C = VV)
new_statements.reading: A categorical, weight-driven rule over the grammatical word: the single heavy syllable (long vowel, glottalised nucleus, or short vowel + fortis consonant reanalysed as VV) is stressed in whatever position it occupies; with two or more heavy syllables, or (loans only) no heavy syllable, stress defaults to the penult; loans with no heavy syllable but a closed syllable stress the last closed syllable. Tone is irrelevant; prefixes are not mentioned as stress-bearing (all examples with prefixes stress the root). This is the explicit algorithm behind the JIPA 2010 hedge ('usually penultimate of the root.. weight also affects placement.. final diphthongs/laryngealized vowels attract stress'): it agrees with every JIPA clause and adds that the weight attraction is general (any position, not only final) and exceptionless in the 1944-50 data. It supports, and if anything strengthens, the 'weight' half of the current 'weight-hedged' coding; the hedge itself is JIPA's own 'usually/exceptions', which Pickett 1951 does not share.

new_statements.quote: Como el español, el diidxazá tiene contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica. [Cuadro 6: ridxi 'ruido' (palabra grave) / ridxí' 'de día' (palabra aguda); riga 'cáscara' / rigá 'se corta'; naga' 'atorado' / nagá' 'verde, frondoso'] ... Las mismas reglas que rigen la representación ortográfica del acento en español son válidas para las palabras del diidxazá. Por eso, como la gran mayoría de ellas tienen acento en la penúltima sílaba y terminan en vocal, no escribimos acento ortográfico. No se escribe el acento ortográfico sobre las vocales quebradas porque siempre forman una sílaba tónica.
new_statements.translation: Like Spanish, Diidxazá has contrasts between words by the position of the stressed syllable. [Table 6: ridxi 'noise' (penult-stressed) / ridxí' 'by day' (final-stressed); riga 'peel' / rigá 'it gets cut'; naga' 'stuck' / nagá' 'green, leafy'] ... The same rules that govern the orthographic representation of stress in Spanish are valid for the words of Diidxazá. Therefore, since the great majority of them have stress on the penultimate syllable and end in a vowel, we do not write an orthographic accent. The orthographic accent is not written on broken (long) vowels because they always form a stressed syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog/Pickett 1951 on the penult default and on heavy (long/broken) nuclei always being stressed, and adds the phonetic correlates of the tonic syllable, the restriction of V'/VV nuclei to tonic syllables, and phrasal stress reduction in compounds. One tension: the grammar frames stress position as contrastive ('contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica') and lists pairs (riga/rigá, naga'/nagá') that are not derivable from its own vowel-type statement, whereas Pickett 1951 argues stress is fully predictable from complex nuclei; the popular orthography's V/V'/VV may under-differentiate the 1951 nucleus types, so this may be orthographic rather than a real…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default penultimate stress ('la gran mayoría' penult, vowel-final); syllables with a broken/long vowel (VV) are always stressed; the stressed syllable may carry any of the three nucleus types V, V', VV, while unstressed syllables have mainly simple V (the glottalised V' only utterance-medially, VV never) (p. 16). Stress position also distinguishes some word pairs (grave vs aguda, Cuadro 6). Phonetic correlates of the tonic syllable: simple vowel lengthened word-finally or before a weak consonant, a following fortis consonant lengthened, low tone dips slightly and is a bit higher than the next syllable (p. 16). The grammar states no algorithm for the aguda cases.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None for the word. Phrase/compound level: when two words join in a phrase or compound, only the final (main) word's tonic syllable keeps all tonic features and the other tonic syllables become atonic, e.g. ba'du' + huiini' -> ba'duhuiini' pronounced [baduhuiini'] (p. 17; Apéndice p. 124, Cuadro 45).
new_statements.exceptions: Word pairs contrasting by stress position (Cuadro 6, p. 16): ridxi/ridxí', riga/rigá, naga'/nagá'; monosyllables like cá 'pegado, escrito' vs the clitics ca 'PL' / ca 'ese', and bé 'moho' vs the dependent pronoun be 'él, ella', which differ in phrasal stress (pp. 16-17). Vowel-initial words are rare and a few begin with a tonic vowel (ique 'cabeza', iza 'año', p. 14). Tones (sec. 3.4, p. 13) are separate from stress: every syllable has a tone (low, high, rising) and tone alone can distinguish words (ruchaa 'cambia' vs ruchaa 'recalienta').
new_statements.identity_note: The grammar describes the Isthmus Zapotec (diidxazá, ISO zai) of Juchitán, Oaxaca; it notes (p. 13) that its tone markings follow Juchitán speakers and that Tehuantepec and other towns differ in tone. First edition printed June 1998, second (electronic) edition March 2001; the two listed works are one and the same item.

new_statements.quote: Los rasgos de contraste entre la sílaba tónica y la átona son los siguientes: Sílaba tónica: • Tiene cualquiera de los tres tipos de vocales: V, V', VV. • La vocal sencilla se alarga en sílaba final o ante consonante débil. • La consonante fuerte se alarga cuando sigue a una sílaba tónica. • El tono bajo desciende ligeramente en la sílaba tónica, y es un poco más alto que la sílaba siguiente. Sílaba átona: • Tiene principalmente la vocal sencilla; la vocal cortada se presenta sólo en medio de la emisión, y la quebrada no aparece en sílaba átona.
new_statements.translation: The contrasting features of the stressed and the unstressed syllable are the following: Stressed syllable: • It has any of the three vowel types: V, V', VV. • The simple vowel is lengthened in a final syllable or before a weak consonant. • The fortis consonant is lengthened when it follows a stressed syllable. • Low tone falls slightly in the stressed syllable and is a little higher than the following syllable. Unstressed syllable: • It has mainly the simple vowel; the cut (glottalised) vowel appears only in the middle of the utterance, and the broken (long) vowel does not occur in an unstressed syllable.

tone_statements.quote: Como en el caso de otras lenguas zapotecas, el diidxazá presenta tono y voz vocálica contrastivos, así como acento prosódico predecible. El idioma cuenta con tres tonos: un tono bajo (o falta de tono), que es el de mayor frecuencia, un tono alto y un tono ascendente. Hay tres tipos de vocales: modal (V), cortada (V’) y rearticulada (VV). El Alfabeto Popular representa la voz vocálica a nivel ortográfico, tal como se acaba de mostrar entre paréntesis, pero no representa el tono. [...] La raíz léxica tiene como forma canónica CV(CV), a la cual se le asigna acento prosódico invariable en la primera sílaba.
tone_statements.translation: As in other Zapotec languages, Diidxazá has contrastive tone and vowel phonation, as well as predictable prosodic stress. The language has three tones: a low tone (or absence of tone), which is the most frequent, a high tone and a rising tone. There are three vowel types: modal (V), checked (V') and rearticulated (VV). The Alfabeto Popular represents vowel phonation orthographically, as just shown in parentheses, but does not represent tone. [...] The lexical root has the canonical shape CV(CV), to which invariable prosodic stress is assigned on the first syllable.
tone_statements.locator: p. 146, section 'Características de la fonología de la lengua'; last sentence p. 147

tone_statements.quote: All are either short [a] or long [a·]. They have either a middle [a], a high [á] or a low [à] pitch. Vowels are either glottalized [a’], aspirated [a‘], nasalized [a,] or rearticulated [aᵃ]. [...] The final vowel of the absolute is almost always low or middle in pitch; that of the non-absolute forms varies, the first person singular always being high, the second low, and the third either high or middle, generally high. In the very few cases where the final vowel of the absolute is high that of the non-absolute forms is either middle or low. Without a clear realization of these tone patterns Zapotec grammar is unintelligible.

readall_conflicts: Placement agrees across sources (penult default, long/broken nuclei attract stress), but the type differs: the 2001 Gramática popular (sec. 3.6, p. 16) says Diidxazá, like Spanish, 'tiene contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica' and lists grave/aguda pairs (ridxi/ridxí', riga/rigá, naga'/nagá'), two of which cannot be derived from the vowel-type generalisation the grammar itself gives (riga and rigá both show simple vowels; naga' and nagá' both show a final cut vowel), whereas Pickett 1951 (word 7:60-65, p. 65) concludes that stress is predictable from complex nuclei and closed syllables and is nonphonemic given word boundaries. The popular orthography's three-way V/V'/VV may not encode all the nucleus distinctions of the 1951 phonemic analysis, so the disagreement may be orthographic; the grammar does not itself claim unpredictability. The catalog's 'weight-hedged penult' coding is consistent with both.

sources.quote: Stress has been posited for Isthmus Zapotec; it affects the length of the vowel itself (before lenis consonants), or the length of the consonant that follows (if it is fortis), or the tone (see Conventions). It usually falls on the penultimate (or the only) syllable of the root when the vowels are modal, although there are exceptions. Convincing examples clearly showing that the generalization is not appropriately stated as referring to the first syllable of the root are not easy to come by since stems longer than two syllables often seem to be compounds or to derive from compounds. The word /wakaaba/ ... ‘a particularly venomous tarantula’ may be an appropriate example. The weight of a syllable also affects the placement of stress. Final diphthongs attract stress: ... ‘reed (otate)’. Final laryngealized vowels also attract stress: ... ‘woman’. Stress does not occur on the prefix of a w…

sources.quote: Stress falls (1) on the syllable containing a complex nucleus in words with one and only one such syllable, (2) on the penultimate syllable (a) in words containing two or more syllables each with complex nucleus and (b) in words containing only open syllables each with simple nucleus, (3) on the last closed syllable of words with no syllable of complex nucleus but with one or more closed syllables. Thus we conclude that for both words of native origin and loan words, stress is predictable in Isthmus Zapotec.

sources.quote: Como el español, el diidxazá tiene contraste entre palabras por la posición de la sílaba tónica. [Cuadro 6: ridxi 'ruido' (palabra grave) / ridxí' 'de día' (palabra aguda); riga 'cáscara' / rigá 'se corta'; naga' 'atorado' / nagá' 'verde, frondoso'] ... Las mismas reglas que rigen la representación ortográfica del acento en español son válidas para las palabras del diidxazá. Por eso, como la gran mayoría de ellas tienen acento en la penúltima sílaba y terminan en vocal, no escribimos acento ortográfico. No se escribe el acento ortográfico sobre las vocales quebradas porque siempre forman una sílaba tónica.

sources.quote: Los rasgos de contraste entre la sílaba tónica y la átona son los siguientes: Sílaba tónica: • Tiene cualquiera de los tres tipos de vocales: V, V', VV. • La vocal sencilla se alarga en sílaba final o ante consonante débil. • La consonante fuerte se alarga cuando sigue a una sílaba tónica. • El tono bajo desciende ligeramente en la sílaba tónica, y es un poco más alto que la sílaba siguiente. Sílaba átona: • Tiene principalmente la vocal sencilla; la vocal cortada se presenta sólo en medio de la emisión, y la quebrada no aparece en sílaba átona.

sources.quote: All are either short [a] or long [a·]. They have either a middle [a], a high [á] or a low [à] pitch. Vowels are either glottalized [a’], aspirated [a‘], nasalized [a,] or rearticulated [aᵃ]. [...] The final vowel of the absolute is almost always low or middle in pitch; that of the non-absolute forms varies, the first person singular always being high, the second low, and the third either high or middle, generally high. In the very few cases where the final vowel of the absolute is high that of the non-absolute forms is either middle or low. Without a clear realization of these tone patterns Zapotec grammar is unintelligible.

sources.citation: Pérez Báez, Gabriela, Víctor Cata & Juan José Bueno Holle. 2015. Xneza diidxazá: retos en la escritura del zapoteco del Istmo vistos desde el texto Teria. Tlalocan 20: 135-172. doi:10.19130/iifl.tlalocan.2015.241
sources.quote: Como en el caso de otras lenguas zapotecas, el diidxazá presenta tono y voz vocálica contrastivos, así como acento prosódico predecible. El idioma cuenta con tres tonos: un tono bajo (o falta de tono), que es el de mayor frecuencia, un tono alto y un tono ascendente. Hay tres tipos de vocales: modal (V), cortada (V’) y rearticulada (VV). El Alfabeto Popular representa la voz vocálica a nivel ortográfico, tal como se acaba de mostrar entre paréntesis, pero no representa el tono. [...] La raíz léxica tiene como forma canónica CV(CV), a la cual se le asigna acento prosódico invariable en la primera sílaba.
sources.locator: p. 146, section 'Características de la fonología de la lengua'; last sentence p. 147
sources.note: Orthography/phonological-word paper with a first-hand phonology section: Diidxazá has contrastive tone and contrastive vowel phonation plus predictable stress; three tones — low (or toneless, the most frequent), high and rising; the 1956 Alfabeto Popular does not write tone, and an INALI-backed norm in preparation will add diacritics for high and rising (low unmarked); interlinear examples give a surface IPA line 'mostrando tono sandhi'; stress is invariably on the first syllable of the CV(CV) root and in compounds falls on the rightmost phonological word.

tone.quote: Como en el caso de otras lenguas zapotecas, el diidxazá presenta tono y voz vocálica contrastivos, así como acento prosódico predecible. El idioma cuenta con tres tonos: un tono bajo (o falta de tono), que es el de mayor frecuencia, un tono alto y un tono ascendente. Hay tres tipos de vocales: modal (V), cortada (V’) y rearticulada (VV). El Alfabeto Popular representa la voz vocálica a nivel ortográfico, tal como se acaba de mostrar entre paréntesis, pero no representa el tono. [...] La raíz léxica tiene como forma canónica CV(CV), a la cual se le asigna acento prosódico invariable en la primera sílaba.
tone.locator: p. 146, section 'Características de la fonología de la lengua'; last sentence p. 147
tone.translation: As in other Zapotec languages, Diidxazá has contrastive tone and vowel phonation, as well as predictable prosodic stress. The language has three tones: a low tone (or absence of tone), which is the most frequent, a high tone and a rising tone. There are three vowel types: modal (V), checked (V') and rearticulated (VV). The Alfabeto Popular represents vowel phonation orthographically, as just shown in parentheses, but does not represent tone. [...] The lexical root has the canonical shape CV(CV), to which invariable prosodic stress is assigned on the first syllable.
